claims.heading: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
claims.claim: Short access-token lifetimes make revocation of access tokens matter less, which moves the risk to the long-lived **refresh token**: it carries the client's full grant and is not tied to one API, so a stolen, replayable refresh token lets an attacker mint new access tokens ✅[^3]

claims.heading: ## 6. Revocation mechanisms
claims.claim: Short access tokens limit how long a revoked grant can still be used ✅[^6]
claims.context: Short access tokens limit how long a revoked grant can still be used ✅[^6], which is why most designs keep them to minutes and accept that window ⚠️ unverified. Worked number: with a 15-minute lifetime, a token issued at 09:30:00 and a logout at 09:40:00 leave a 5-minute window (until 09:45:00); a token issued at 09:39:59 leaves almost the full 15 minutes.

claims.heading: ## 6. Revocation mechanisms
claims.claim: Node.js's `Buffer` decoder for `base64url` accepts the regular base64 alphabet by design ✅[^20]
claims.context: - **Lenient base64url decoding.** A 32-byte HS256 signature is 43 base64url characters, 258 bits for 256 bits of data, so the last character carries 2 unused bits; lenient decoders also accept `=` padding and the `+`/`/` alphabet ✅[^5]. Node.js's `Buffer` decoder for `base64url` accepts the regular base64 alphabet by design ✅[^20]. In the lab, five altered strings of one HS256 token all verified with a lenient decoder, none was on the hash denylist, and a strict decoder that re-encodes and compares rejected all five ✅[^24].

claims.heading: ## 6. Revocation mechanisms
claims.claim: - D3: rotation detects nothing when the legitimate client never presents its last token again, which is why RFC 10017 says rotation alone does not stop persistent theft ✅[^2]
claims.context: - D3: rotation detects nothing when the legitimate client never presents its last token again, which is why RFC 10017 says rotation alone does not stop persistent theft ✅[^2]. An inactivity expiry, which RFC 9700 says refresh tokens should have ✅[^3], bounds this case: with a 30-minute inactivity limit, the thief's attempt one hour later would fail.

claims.heading: ## 6. Revocation mechanisms
claims.claim: Each request carries a DPoP proof: a JWT with header `typ: dpop+jwt` and the public key, and claims `jti`, `htm` (method), `htu` (URL), `iat`, plus `ath` (hash of the access token) and the server's `nonce` when required ✅[^11]
claims.context: Analogy: a bank card that also needs a PIN at every purchase; a copied card number alone buys nothing. The client holds a key pair. Each request carries a DPoP proof: a JWT with header `typ: dpop+jwt` and the public key, and claims `jti`, `htm` (method), `htu` (URL), `iat`, plus `ath` (hash of the access token) and the server's `nonce` when required ✅[^11]. The access token names the key's thumbprint in `cnf.jkt`, and the RS refuses a DPoP-bound token sent as a plain bearer token ✅[^11]. Public clients get refresh tokens bound to the same key ✅[^11].

claims.heading: ## 6. Revocation mechanisms
claims.claim: The OP posts `logout_token=<JWT>` to each client's registered `backchannel_logout_uri`; the client validates it (signature, `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `events` containing `http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout`, `sub` or `sid`, no `nonce`), ends the matching sessions, and answers `200` (or `204`); refresh tokens without `offline_access` should be revoked, those with it normally kept ✅[^9]
claims.context: - **OIDC back-channel logout:** analogy: the hotel's front desk phoning every restaurant where the guest ran a tab, server to server, instead of relying on the guest to walk past each one. The OP posts `logout_token=<JWT>` to each client's registered `backchannel_logout_uri`; the client validates it (signature, `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `events` containing `http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout`, `sub` or `sid`, no `nonce`), ends the matching sessions, and answers `200` (or `204`); refresh tokens without `offline_access` should be revoked, those with it normally kept ✅[^9]. claims.heading: ## 6. Revocation mechanisms
claims.claim: Against malware that copies cookies, Chrome's DBSC has the browser create a per-session key pair in hardware (TPM, Trusted Platform Module, on Windows; Secure Enclave on macOS) and prove possession before the server issues new short-lived cookies; it reached public availability on Windows in Chrome 146, announced 2026-04-09 ✅[^19]
claims.context: Against malware that copies cookies, Chrome's DBSC has the browser create a per-session key pair in hardware (TPM, Trusted Platform Module, on Windows; Secure Enclave on macOS) and prove possession before the server issues new short-lived cookies; it reached public availability on Windows in Chrome 146, announced 2026-04-09 ✅[^19]. A stolen cookie then expires quickly. It is a browser-level form of sender-constraining for cookie sessions and needs the site to add registration and refresh endpoints ✅[^19].
